_meta: A single sample of measurements, used to show that the standard deviation and the standard error answer two different questions and cannot be swapped: the standard deviation (SD) describes how spread out the individual measurements are and is a property of the distribution that does NOT shrink as you collect more data, while the standard error of the mean (SEM = SD / sqrt(n)) describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the true mean and DOES shrink as sqrt(n) with more data. Put an error bar of one SD on the mean and you overstate the mean's uncertainty by a factor of sqrt(n) -- and, absurdly, the bar never tightens no matter how much data you gather. Put an error bar of one SEM around the individuals and you understate their spread by the same factor -- you claim a typical measurement lands in a band that most measurements actually fall outside of. Only a minority of individual points lie within mean +/- SEM, because SEM is not a range for individuals; most lie within mean +/- SD, because SD is. The data is a fixture of n measurements; the mean, sample SD, SEM = SD/sqrt(n), how the SEM would change at 4x and 1/4x the sample size, and how many individual points fall within mean +/- SD versus mean +/- SEM are all computed. Stdlib only.
